Photograph: NSW Police New South Wales From ‘elation’ to ‘terrible news’ in 10 minutes: how the confusion over missing bushwalker Lily Hooper unfolded The 18-year-old’s body was found in Nattai national park on Thursday – but initial police messages indicated she was alive Teen hiker Lily Hooper found dead as NSW police apologise for miscommunication ‘born of elation’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Thu 20 Aug 2026 05.51 EDT Last modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 06.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police have blamed dense bushland and radio confusion for wrongly reporting to 18-year-old Lily Hooper’s parents, the New South Wales premier and the media that the missing bushwalker had been found alive. Hooper had last been seen on 12 August after leaving home for a hike in the rugged bushland of Nattai national park, 90km south-west of Sydney . She was reported missing that night, triggering a multi-agency search involving nearly 1,000 people, including hundreds of volunteers. Missing teen hiker Lily Hooper found dead as NSW police apologise for miscommunication ‘born of elation’ Read more Eight days later, on Thursday morning, police media told reporters a “hiker” had been found. At around midday, the premier, Chris Minns , was handed a piece of paper while addressing a parliamentary committee. He asked if it was accurate, to which the secretary of the cabinet office, Kate Boyd, said: “Yes.” The premier, reading the paper, said he had “fantastic news” that Hooper was “found in the bush with half a bottle of water with her”. His remarks were published across media outlets. Minutes later, Minns told the committee: “I’ve got some terrible news. I apologise … Lily’s body has been found .” Questions immediately centred on how such a serious error could have been made. SES search volunteers had told police they believed they had found Hooper alive at 11.30am, the police assistant commissioner Joseph Cassar told reporters in Moss Vale on Thursday afternoon. Recounting the sequence of communication, he said officers soon shared that message with Hooper’s parents, who had spent a “great deal” of time at the search command post near the head of the Bonnum Pic walking trail, where the teenager’s car had been found. Vehicles drive along road near NSW national park where Lily Hooper’s body was discovered Cassar said the hundreds of searchers, carrying handheld radios, faced communication challenges in the “thick, dense terrain”. They had “clear instructions” to report when they found anything, even an item of clothing, he said. The SES assistant commissioner Colin Malone said the SES volunteers were from the “highly trained” bush search and rescue team. “It’s very rugged and rough terrain up there and radio communication, like mobile phone communication, as we all experience, when you’re in black spots or tricky areas, the information does get broken up a little bit,” Malone said. Within 10 minutes, the same SES volunteers made a second “more accurate” report, Cassar said. He said they would probably have been “very close” to Hooper’s body. By then, the incorrect message had already begun to circulate publicly. The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, told reporters on Thursday afternoon that police had hurried to share the initial report after searching for Hooper for eight days. “We sought to communicate, obviously, with the family and the media at the first opportunity,” Lanyon said. “Elation,” he said, soon turned to “deflation – and obviously we know now, an impact on her family”. “I unashamedly apologise for any additional trauma that may have caused Lily’s family, but certainly for the embarrassment and confusion that caused.” Map showing Bonnum Pic walking trail. Minns later said in a statement that he received incorrect advice and “genuinely believed” he was sharing good news. “My deepest condolences are with Lily’s family,” the premier said. “I am profoundly sorry to think that anything I said may have added to their heartbreak at an already devastating time.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Angus Taylor, the opposition leader, had reportedly published and then deleted a social media post indicating she had been found alive. He addressed the miscommunication while paying tribute to Hooper in parliament. “Initial reports that she had been found alive proved to be wrong and that makes the blow even worse,” Taylor said. Lanyon said police would have reported the finding to the office of the police minister, Yasmin Catley, and then to the premier’s office. “I can’t explain why it was so quick but what I can say to you is this search has been high profile,” he said. Lanyon said he had called Minns to apologise for the “misinformation” he had received. Minns’ reference to a water bottle prompted speculation that search crews had used a code word in their initial report. Asked how the “water bottle” phrase had been referenced, Cassar said: “I can’t tell you because I don’t know exactly what was said.” Nattai national park is about 90km south-west of Sydney. Lanyon said he could not explain the reference but communications would be reviewed and improved. Police, the SES and the premier’s office declined to comment on whether coded terms had been involved in the miscommunication. “This is not a circumstance I would like to see repeated,” Lanyon said. “We will look at the relationship between police and the SES and we’ll work with other agencies to make sure communication failures don’t occur.” The public breakdown in communications came a week after NSW police separately reported finding a “body” inside a suitcase which was determined the next day to have been a sex doll. Lanyon denied the two incidents would impact public perceptions or trust in police. “The police took exactly the right precautions [when] what we now know was a doll was found in a suitcase,” he said. “I accept later on it was [determined] not a body, but I think the community would expect the police to treat crime scenes seriously and preserve evidence, and that’s what was done.” Explore more on these topics New South Wales Angus Taylor Chris Minns Sydney news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Missing teen hiker Lily Hooper found dead as NSW police apologise for miscommunication ‘born of elation’ Two 17-year-olds from Sydney private school among three charged over alleged rape of teenage girl Catholic schools chief denies wiping critical evidence after performing factory reset on phone, Icac hears NSW judge says anti-Israel graffiti case went ‘haywire’ when vandalism was labelled antisemitic Five Sydney Swans players suspended for rest of AFL season say they are ‘deeply sorry’ Full Story Does Australia have a gun problem? – Full Story podcast Sydney Swans will sanction players for ‘serious breach’ over incident that led to sexual assault allegations Family of missing 18-year-old hiker ‘absolutely devastated’ as search continues in rugged NSW terrain Bondi library removes book How to Sell a Genocide from shelves after complaint Sydney Swans coach ‘extremely disappointed’ as club faces call on standing down players linked to alleged sexual assault Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.baltictimes.com/fm__kremlin_.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive FM: Kremlin’s provocations must be countered with extra forces at border, support for Kyiv 2026-09-10 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Following Russia’s attempt to carry out a ‘hybrid attack’ at a German airport using an explosive-laden drone in August, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys states that such and similar provocations by the Kremlin must be countered by deploying additional forces at the border, as well as by increasing support for Ukraine. "When I hear that debate in Europe that perhaps we shouldn’t respond, because we might escalate (the situation), that thinking is based on completely false premises, that is how we think. The Russians do not think that way. If you don’t respond, it means you’re soft, and it means they can do whatever they want with you," Budrys told the Ziniu Radijas news radio on Thursday. "Just as we stopped the sabotage of critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea, we can also stop these diversionary attacks, these acts of terrorism being organized in Europe - with a firm response - including the deployment of additional forces at the border, to show that this is a response. After all, we will not respond symmetrically; we will not organize operations of this nature in Russia. We must increase the support package for Ukraine, and push them (Kremlin’s provocateurs) out of Europe. That is what the response should be," he pointed out. Lithuania’s top diplomat, amongst other things, made a point of emphasizing that some European countries should restrict the issuance of visas to Russian citizens. "Some European countries are increasing the number of visas issued... and for some, tourism and the arrival of Russians - who have nowhere else to spend their money but do so in European restaurants and on beaches - do not seem to be linked to the war. For us, however, it is very directly linked," the minister stressed. Last week, Berlin blamed Moscow for the incident at the Leipzig airport, which the European Union said bore all the hallmarks of "state-sponsored terrorism". In response to the situation, EU countries are considering the possibility of imposing new sanctions. The 21st package has caused damage to the Russian economy, but analysts say that its deterrent effect has been limited so far. https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: Giulio Meotti is an Italian journalist with Il Foglio, a Middle East Forum fellow and writer of a twice-weekly column for Arutz Sheva. He is the author, in English, of the book "A New Shoah", that researched the personal stories of Israel's terror victims, published by Encounter and of "J'Accuse: the Vatican Against Israel" published by Mantua Books, in addition to books in Italian. His writing has appeared in publications, such as the Wall Street Journal, Gatestone, Frontpage and Commentary. The New York Times , which apologized and had to remove after publication an unfortunate sentence from an article on NAZA (the sentence was: “Israelis continue largely to see themselves as victims of October 7"), is the only misstep in an operation chiselled to perfection, with the pro-Palestinian communications machine running at full speed. The documentary by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, in which anonymous voices accuse Israel of genocide, is a kind of “Merchant of Venice" with the IDF in place of Shylock. The creditor who becomes the executioner. Premiere it at one of the world’s most prestigious festivals and show it to a handful of journalists, film critics and celebrities already aligned with political correctness. Late entry into competition: NAZA is announced in Venice on 24 August. “Not bringing it would have been cowardly," says the director of the Venice Film Festival, Alberto Barbera. Win a prize. Beat the applause record. Spark a chorus of enthusiastic reviews that denounce “Israeli genocidal policy." Make sure Israeli politicians and military officials condemn it, with some ministers evoking the loss of citizenship for the two directors. Present that condemnation as further proof of the film’s courage. Ignore Hamas’s enthusiasm for the film as an embarrassing detail; the Israeli condemnation exhibited as further proof of truth. Thus, once fixed on the big screen, a myth is much harder to dismantle. Now the documentary is hailed in the world’s movie theaters. Venice was the perfect stage. Last year it was “The Voice of Hind Rajab" that received a standing ovation of 23 minutes and 50 seconds, later sold to the press as “the longest in the history of film festivals." The film does not take viewers to Gaza, but to Ramallah. The story unfolds in the offices of the Palestinian Arab Red Crescent. We do not see the Gaza neighbourhood from which Hind’s family was fleeing. We do not see Israeli forces, Hamas terrorists, the tunnels, the evacuations or the warnings. The tragedy is severed from the events that precipitated it. The war becomes an abstraction. Responsibility lies only with the Israelis, who are never named. The Jewish State exists only as a faceless, voiceless presence: an invisible force, pure evil. Meanwhile Gal Gadot and Gerard Butler had to give up being seen in Venice. The former because she is Israeli, the latter because he raised funds for the Israeli army. It seems that about a hundred Italian pro-Palestinian Arab actors and directors did not want to see them in Venice and asked that Gadot and Butler be boycotted. No scandal. Then NAZA arrives. 24 and a half minutes of applause, just enough time to surpass “The Voice of Hind Rajab," with director Barbera watching the clock waiting for NAZA to set the new record. Meanwhile Susan Sarandon at 79 donned the clothes of victimhood (“I am excluded from Hollywood because I am pro-Palestinian"). The Guardian , a British newspaper with a glorious past and an ideological present, is the film’s main producer and will now stream it for free. The same Guardian that hosts articles by Marwan Barghouti: serving five life sentences in an Israeli prison not because he dreams of “peace," but because he ordered the killing of many Israelis in the Second Intifada. Since 2 January 2001, the day it published an article by Faisal Bodi titled “Israel has no right to exist," the Guardian has made anti-Israelism an editorial badge of honour. And here the producers of NZA enter the scene. They are the director of the highly awarded “The Zone of Interest," Jonathan Glazer, and his producer, James Wilson. On Oscar night, Glazer caused a scandal by saying he did not want his own Jewishness and the Holocaust used to justify Israel’s war against Hamas. In NAZA coinciding with Israel’s commemoration of the anniversary of the Holocaust, we see the façade of the Tel Aviv Cinematheque and the programme that includes “Shoah," Claude Lanzmann’s masterpiece. Shortly afterwards, one of the military figures who all appear in shadow in the film recalls a trip to Poland with his family to honour the memory of his ancestors who were exterminated and then says: “The Nazis were the devil, but what am I?" A refined blow. The Shoah is not denied: it is used as a mirror for Israel. There is no need to erase Auschwitz. It is enough to reflect it onto Israel. But Lanzmann, who died in 2018 in Paris, was one of the filmmakers most committed to Israel’s defence and also made a five-hour documentary titled “Tsahal" on the Israeli army. The analogy with “The Zone of Interest" is taken up by Guardian columnist Arwa Mahdawi in an article published on 12 June this year, referring to an advertisement by actress Gwyneth Paltrow for a residential complex in Herzliya. The thesis is that Israeli civilians living eighty kilometres from Gaza are complicit in Nazi-style evil. Also involved in NAZA is +972 Magazine, an Israeli far-left outlet which has received grants from the Open Society Foundations every year from 2018 to 2024, totalling $562,900. George Soros’s Open Society has always been aligned against Israel. It is not a conspiracy. It is an ecosystem. This does not prove that Soros and the Open Society financed NAZA. But the funding and the context are not irrelevant. Apart from reader donations, over the years the magazine that produced NAZA has also received funding from foreign foundations linked to progressive causes (“How we are funded" on their site is very transparent), such as the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation and the Heinrich Böll Foundation. The latter is linked to the Green Party in Germany. Let me repeat: It is not a conspiracy, it is an ecosystem. This year a film financed by Qatar (a financier of Hamas) through the Doha Film Institute, “La Maison du Vent," instead won the Lion of the Future in Venice. Of more than eighty films in contention this year on the Lido, eight were projects supported by the Doha Film Institute. And here we return to NAZA. Because James Wilson, one of the producers of NAZA and Jonathan Glazer, its executive producer, are also the producers of “The Voice of Hind Rajab," financed by the Doha Film Institute. It does not matter that Israel dropped seven million leaflets on Gaza, made more than seventy thousand direct phone calls, sent more than thirteen million text messages and left more than fifteen million pre-recorded voice messages to inform civilians of the need to leave combat zones, indicating where to go and which route to follow, or that it used drones equipped with loudspeakers. None of this matters to those who accuse Israel of “genocide." Who built the tunnels? Who occupied them? Who stored weapons there and held innocents hostage? Who declared that the tunnels were meant for fighters rather than civilians? Not relevant. The twenty-five minutes of applause for NAZA were not for the film: they allowed Venice’s cultured and well-off audience to reassure themselves of their anti-Zionist passion (but not antisemitic, they repeat, since they always find a Jew ready to blame his own people). Would they have applauded an Israeli documentary that described with the same meticulousness Hamas’s methods, the 1,200 Israelis killed in less than three hours, the thousands of tunnels dug under Gaza? Would the Venice hall have stood up? Someone, perhaps. Perhaps twenty-five seconds. Because, to put it in the words of Soviet writer Sergei Dovlatov, “progressive humanity demands of Israel a noble suicide." The next anti-Israel applause in Venice will last twenty-six minutes.
